<meta>continues from previous page: describing a violent altercation where someone was beaten with boards and sticks while standing, leaving two gashes on their face.</meta>

"They used boards and sticks on him while he was standing there. I do not know what implement was used, but he was beaten severely, and his face was cut in two places. We heard that your mother has a certain type of medicine here for treating staff wounds <note>The 'staff' or 'board' was the standard instrument for corporal punishment in a domestic or legal setting.</note>. Would you look for a pill to give me, Miss?"

When Bao-chai heard this, she quickly ordered Ying-er to find two pills and give them to Ping-er. Bao-chai said, "Since this is the case, please convey my regards to her on my behalf. I shall not go myself." Ping-er gave her word to Bao-chai and departed. This matter requires no further comment.

We turn now to Xiang-ling. After meeting the others and finishing her evening meal, she saw Bao-chai and the rest leave for her mother’s quarters. Xiang-ling then made her way to the瀟湘館 <term>Xiaoxiang Guan</term> <gloss>The Bamboo Lodge, residence of Lin Dai-yu</gloss>. By this time, Dai-yu was mostly recovered from her illness. Seeing Xiang-ling come into the garden to live, she was naturally pleased. Xiang-ling said with a smile, "Now that I have moved in and have some free time, if you would only teach me how to compose poetry, it would be my great good fortune!"

Dai-yu smiled and replied, "Since you want to learn to compose poetry, you must acknowledge me as your master. Although I am not an expert, I know enough to teach you the basics." Xiang-ling laughed, "If that is truly the case, I shall take you as my master. You must not grow weary of me."

Dai-yu said, "What difficulty is there in this that makes it worth such fuss? It is nothing more than the four stages: the opening, the development, the transition, and the conclusion <note>original: "qi cheng zhuan he," the structural requirement for regulated verse</note>. Within the development and transition sections, there are two pairs of couplets. Tonal level sounds must be matched against deflected sounds; empty words against solid words, and solid words against empty words <note>This refers to the grammatical and tonal parallelism required in Chinese poetry, where 'solid' words are nouns and 'empty' words are particles or abstract terms</note>. If you truly have a brilliant line, you may even disregard these rules of tone and structure."

Xiang-ling laughed, "No wonder when I occasionally steal a look at one or two poems in old books, some couplets are perfectly matched while others are not. I also heard people say, 'the first, third, and fifth syllables do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be precise.' Yet in the poems of the ancients, some follow this and some are wrong in the even-numbered positions. I have been confused every day. Now that I hear you speak, it seems these rules are not so rigid after all, as long as the phrasing is fresh and original."

Dai-yu said, "That is exactly the principle. Phrasing is ultimately a secondary matter; the most important thing is the conception. If the intent and flavor are authentic, the poem will be good even without polished phrasing. This is what is called 'not letting the words damage the meaning.'"

Xiang-ling said, "I simply love Lu Fang-weng's <note>Lu You, a famous Southern Song dynasty poet</note> lines: 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, keeping the fragrance long; the ancient inkstone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It is so vivid and interesting!"

Dai-yu replied, "It is because you do not yet understand poetry that you love such shallow and accessible things. Once you fall into that pattern, you will never be able to break out of it to learn better things. Listen to me: if you truly wish to learn, I have here the *Collected Works of Wang Mo-jie* <note>Wang Wei, a Tang dynasty master known for his Buddhist-influenced nature poetry</note>. Take his hundred five-character regulated verses and study them until you have thoroughly mastered them. Then read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's <note>Du Fu, the 'Poet-Historian' of the Tang dynasty</note> seven-character regulated verses. After that, read one or two hundred of Li Qing-lian's <note>Li Bai, the 'Poet-Immortal' of the Tang dynasty</note> seven-character quatrains. Once you have these three men as your foundation, you can look at Tao Yuan-ming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, Bao, and the others. With a person as clever and bright as you are, in less than a year, you need not worry about becoming a true poet!"

Hearing this, Xiang-ling smiled, "In that case, dear Miss, please bring the book out for me. I will take it back and read a few poems tonight." At these words, Dai-yu ordered Zi-juan to bring Wang the Right Vice-President’s <note>An official title for Wang Wei</note> five-character regulated verses. Handing them to Xiang-ling, she said, "Only read the ones marked with red circles; those are the ones I have selected. Read them one by one. If there is anything you do not understand, ask your mistress Bao-chai, or if you see me, I will explain it to you."

Xiang-ling took the poems and returned to the 蘅蕪院 <term>Hengwu Yuan</term> <gloss>The All-Spice Court, residence of Xue Bao-chai</gloss>. Ignoring all other affairs, she began to read them one by one under the lamp. Bao-chai urged her to go to sleep several times, but she would not. Seeing her so devoted, Bao-chai had no choice but to let her be.

One day, just as Dai-yu had finished her morning washing and grooming, Xiang-ling arrived with a beaming face to return the book and ask for the poems of Du Fu. Dai-yu smiled and asked, "How many do you remember?" Xiang-ling laughed, "I have read all of those marked with red circles." Dai-yu asked, "Have you gained any insights?" Xiang-ling smiled, "I have gained some understanding, but I do not know if it is correct. Let me tell you what I think."

<summary>Xiang-ling moves into the Grand Prospect Garden and asks Lin Dai-yu to teach her how to compose poetry. Dai-yu provides a curriculum focused on Tang dynasty masters and emphasizes that poetic meaning is more important than rigid formal rules.</summary>
<keywords>Xiang-ling, Lin Dai-yu, poetry, Wang Wei, Du Fu, Li Bai, literary education, Grand Prospect Garden, regulated verse</keywords>
